The **Conservative Party of Canada** (**CPC**; French: _Parti conservateur du Canada_; **_PCC_**), sometimes referred to as the **Tories**, is a federal political party in Canada. The party sits at the centre-right to right of the Canadian political spectrum, with their federal rival, the centre to centre-leftLiberal Party of Canada, positioned to their left.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Canadian_Encyclopedia-4) The Conservatives are defined as a "big tent" party, practicing "brokerage politics"[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-politics-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Brooks2004-8)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Johnson2016c-9)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Smith2014-10) and welcoming a broad variety of members, including "Red Tories" and "Blue Tories".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Wolak2014-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BellKulchyski2013-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-GagnonTanguay2017-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-LewisEveritt2017-14)

The CPC was formed by the merger of the two main right-leaning parties, the Progressive Conservative Party (PC Party) and the Canadian Alliance. The PC Party's roots go back to the original Conservative Party of Canada, which had formed numerous governments dating back to Canadian Confederation in 1867. In the 1993 federal election, the PC Party's Western Canadian support transferred to the Reform Party, which later became the Canadian Alliance. When it became clear that neither the PC Party nor the Canadian Alliance could beat the incumbent Liberals that had governed since the 1993 election, an effort to unite the right-of-centre parties emerged. In 2003, the Canadian Alliance and the PCs merged, forming the Conservative Party of Canada.
During the Conservative Party's governance of Canada from 2006 to 2015, its economic policies included reducing sales tax, reducing income taxes, reducing business taxes, balancing the national budget, permitting the construction of several pipelines, and creating the tax-free savings account (TFSA) and the Universal Child Care Benefit. In social policy, the government eliminated the long-gun registry, introduced mandatory minimum sentences for violent crimes, and raised the age of consent to 16 years of age. Internationally it supported the State of Israel, withdrew Canada from the Kyoto Protocol, and negotiated the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-18)

Under its first leader, Stephen Harper, the party governed with two minority governments after the federal elections of 2006 and 2008. It then won a majority government in the 2011 federal election before being defeated in the 2015 federal election by a majority Liberal government led by Justin Trudeau. Despite winning a plurality of the vote in each election, the party remained as Official Opposition after losing the 2019 and 2021 elections under its second and third leaders, Andrew Scheer and [Erin O'Toole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_O'Toole "Erin O'Toole") respectively. Pierre Poilievre was elected leader in the 2022 leadership election, leading the party through the 2025 election, which it again lost to the Liberals, while retaining opposition status.
John A. Macdonald, Prime Minister (1867–1873, 1878–1891), Canada's first Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal-Conservative Party, one of the party's predecessors
The Conservative Party is political heir to a series of right-of-centre parties that have existed in Canada, beginning with the Upper Canada Tories of the nineteenth century. John A. Macdonald and George-Étienne Cartier later founded the Liberal-Conservative Party. The party became known simply as the Conservative Party after 1873, and the Progressive Conservative Party after 1942. Like its historical predecessors and conservative parties in some other Commonwealth nations (such as the Conservative Party of the United Kingdom), members of the present-day Conservative Party of Canada are sometimes referred to as "Tories".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Tories-roots-19) The modern Conservative Party of Canada is also legal heir to the heritage of the historical conservative parties by virtue of assuming the assets and liabilities of the former Progressive Conservative Party upon the merger of 2003.

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Erin O'Toole (2020–2022)
Prime Minister Trudeau called the September 2021 federal election in the hopes of winning a majority government, though in the middle of the campaign O'Toole's Conservatives were tied with the Liberals, if not slightly ahead of the Liberals in the polls. During the campaign, O'Toole stated he would balance the budget within the next 10 years[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-52) and reversed his support for repealing the Liberal government's "assault-style" weapons ban.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-53) In a similar manner to the 2019 election, the Conservatives again won the popular vote but fell short of gaining the largest amount of seats, enabling the Liberal Party under Justin Trudeau to form another minority government.
As a result, party members were undecided on whether he should continue as leader.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-54)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-55) On October 5, the Conservative caucus voted to adopt the provisions of the _Reform Act_, giving caucus the power to trigger a leadership review. O'Toole denied that it represented a threat to his leadership, insisting that the caucus was united as a team and that, as a supporter of the Act, he had encouraged his caucus to adopt all of its provisions.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-56)

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Erin O'Toole (2020–2022)
On January 31, 2022, Conservative Calgary Heritage MP Bob Benzen submitted a letter with signatures from 35 Conservative MPs calling for a leadership review on O'Toole's leadership to the Conservative caucus chair, Scott Reid. In the letter, Benzen criticized O'Toole's reversal on repealing the Liberal government's carbon tax and assault weapons ban.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-57) On February 2, 2022, O'Toole was removed as leader by a margin of 73 to 45 votes.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-58)

### In opposition (2015–present)

[edit]

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Second interim leadership (2022)
Then-deputy leader of the Conservative Party Candice Bergen was elected interim leader the same day O'Toole was ousted,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-59) and a leadership election was subsequently scheduled for September 10, 2022. Conservative MP and former cabinet minister Pierre Poilievre,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-runforpm-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-pierre-61) Conservative MP and former leadership candidate Leslyn Lewis,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-62) Independent (formerly Progressive Conservative) Member of Ontario Provincial Parliament Roman Baber,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-63) former leader of the now-defunct Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and former Premier of QuebecJean Charest,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-64) former MP, former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario, and Mayor of BramptonPatrick Brown,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-65) former Conservative MP Leona Alleslev,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-66) former BC MLA and Conservative MP Marc Dalton, and former Huntsville mayor and Conservative MP Scott Aitchison announced their candidacies for the leadership.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-67) On May 2, 2022, the Party announced that the six verified candidates for the leadership would be Aitchison, Baber, Brown, Charest, Lewis, Poilievre.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-68)

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Second interim leadership (2022)
On July 6, 2022, the Party announced that Patrick Brown had been disqualified "due to 'serious allegations of wrongdoing' that 'appear' to violate Canadian election law."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-69) In response, Brown hired lawyer Marie Henein, who requested the Party's dispute resolution appeal committee be convened.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-70)

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
[edit]
On September 10, 2022, Pierre Poilievre won the leadership on the first ballot in a landslide, winning over 68% of the points.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-:7-71) On September 12, Poilievre gave his first speech to his caucus as leader.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-72) On April 28, 2025, the party would lose the 2025 Canadian federal election, despite making parliamentary gains through victories in places such as Ontario, such as the province's 905 area and southwestern region, and receiving over 40% of the popular vote for the first time in party history.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-73)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-74) The Conservatives also formed the largest Official Opposition in Canadian history.

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
Poilievre however lost his own seat of Carleton to Liberal candidate Bruce Fanjoy, one of the few times a major party leader in Canada has been defeated in his own riding.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-loss-2025-76) There were also calls for Poilievre to resign as Conservative leader grew following the election result.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-78) Despite this, there was reportedly limited interest from the party's caucus in replacing him immediately after the election given their party's increase in the share of the vote, expansion of its political base in the Greater Toronto Area, and his own popularity with such across the country.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-79) Prominent Conservative Party MPs including Andrew Scheer, Shannon Stubbs, and former cabinet ministers Jason Kenney and James Moore also publicly supported his continued leadership after the election.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-80) Despite this, he was criticized by veteran and senior party members for his demeanour and campaign management that they cited as a reason for the party's loss of the election.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-81) Poilievre returned to Parliament in August 2025, following his victory in the Battle River—Crowfoot by-election.

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
On November 5, 2025, MP [Chris d'Entremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_d'Entremont "Chris d'Entremont") left the Conservative Party to join the Liberal Party of Canada, citing issues with Pierre Poilievre's leadership style and 'negative' approach to politics; this was followed by MP Michael Ma in December 2025, MP Matt Jeneroux in February 2026, and MP Marilyn Gladu in April 2026.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-82) At the party's convention in Calgary in January 2026, Poilievre received 87.4% support in a leadership review vote, vowing to remain as party leader.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-83)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-84)

## Principles and policies
[edit]
As a relatively young party with a mixed political heritage and history, the federal Conservatives are often described as a "big tent" party[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-CartyTent-85) in a similar manner to the federal Canadian Liberals by encompassing members and voters who hold a variety of philosophies, ideas and stances, albeit sitting within the centre-right to the right-wing of the political spectrum.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-House2015-86)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BlaisLaslier2016-87)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BittnerKoop2013b-88)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Canadian_Encyclopedia-4) Broadly, the party is defined as practicing the Canadian model of conservatism and fiscal conservatism. Some political observers have noted the two most dominant wings of the party traditionally represented Red Tory and Blue Tory ideologies,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-89) whereas others have argued that the party has become less internally defined by these labels and that the terms tend to be used by outsiders.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-90) Other smaller but visible factional beliefs espoused by individuals within the party have been described by media commentators as liberal conservative, social conservative, right-wing populist and libertarian conservative.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-91)

## Principles and policies
In an effort to create a cohesive platform following its creation, the Conservative Party declared its founding core philosophies and principles to be fiscal accountability, upholding individual rights and freedom, belief in constitutional monarchy, the institutions of Parliament and Canada's democratic process, support for strong national defence, law and order, and Canada's history and traditions, and equal treatment for all Canadians.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-ReferenceA-92)

There is no official youth wing of the Conservative Party of Canada. There have been several attempts to create one, but all have failed. texts.1: The **Conservative Party of Canada** (**CPC**; French: _Parti conservateur du Canada_; **_PCC_**), sometimes referred to as the **Tories**, is a federal political party in Canada. The party sits at the centre-right to right of the Canadian political spectrum, with their federal rival, the centre to centre-leftLiberal Party of Canada, positioned to their left.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Canadian_Encyclopedia-4) The Conservatives are defined as a "big tent" party, practicing "brokerage politics"[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-politics-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Brooks2004-8)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Johnson2016c-9)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Smith2014-10) and welcoming a broad variety of members, including "Red Tories" and "Blue Tories".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Wolak2014-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BellKulchyski2013-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-GagnonTanguay2017-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-LewisEveritt2017-14)
texts.2:
The CPC was formed by the merger of the two main right-leaning parties, the Progressive Conservative Party (PC Party) and the Canadian Alliance. The PC Party's roots go back to the original Conservative Party of Canada, which had formed numerous governments dating back to Canadian Confederation in 1867. In the 1993 federal election, the PC Party's Western Canadian support transferred to the Reform Party, which later became the Canadian Alliance. When it became clear that neither the PC Party nor the Canadian Alliance could beat the incumbent Liberals that had governed since the 1993 election, an effort to unite the right-of-centre parties emerged. In 2003, the Canadian Alliance and the PCs merged, forming the Conservative Party of Canada.
During the Conservative Party's governance of Canada from 2006 to 2015, its economic policies included reducing sales tax, reducing income taxes, reducing business taxes, balancing the national budget, permitting the construction of several pipelines, and creating the tax-free savings account (TFSA) and the Universal Child Care Benefit. In social policy, the government eliminated the long-gun registry, introduced mandatory minimum sentences for violent crimes, and raised the age of consent to 16 years of age. Internationally it supported the State of Israel, withdrew Canada from the Kyoto Protocol, and negotiated the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-18)
texts.3:
Under its first leader, Stephen Harper, the party governed with two minority governments after the federal elections of 2006 and 2008. It then won a majority government in the 2011 federal election before being defeated in the 2015 federal election by a majority Liberal government led by Justin Trudeau. Despite winning a plurality of the vote in each election, the party remained as Official Opposition after losing the 2019 and 2021 elections under its second and third leaders, Andrew Scheer and [Erin O'Toole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_O'Toole "Erin O'Toole") respectively. Pierre Poilievre was elected leader in the 2022 leadership election, leading the party through the 2025 election, which it again lost to the Liberals, while retaining opposition status.
John A. Macdonald, Prime Minister (1867–1873, 1878–1891), Canada's first Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal-Conservative Party, one of the party's predecessors
The Conservative Party is political heir to a series of right-of-centre parties that have existed in Canada, beginning with the Upper Canada Tories of the nineteenth century. John A. Macdonald and George-Étienne Cartier later founded the Liberal-Conservative Party. The party became known simply as the Conservative Party after 1873, and the Progressive Conservative Party after 1942. Like its historical predecessors and conservative parties in some other Commonwealth nations (such as the Conservative Party of the United Kingdom), members of the present-day Conservative Party of Canada are sometimes referred to as "Tories".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Tories-roots-19) The modern Conservative Party of Canada is also legal heir to the heritage of the historical conservative parties by virtue of assuming the assets and liabilities of the former Progressive Conservative Party upon the merger of 2003.

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Erin O'Toole (2020–2022)
Prime Minister Trudeau called the September 2021 federal election in the hopes of winning a majority government, though in the middle of the campaign O'Toole's Conservatives were tied with the Liberals, if not slightly ahead of the Liberals in the polls. During the campaign, O'Toole stated he would balance the budget within the next 10 years[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-52) and reversed his support for repealing the Liberal government's "assault-style" weapons ban.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-53) In a similar manner to the 2019 election, the Conservatives again won the popular vote but fell short of gaining the largest amount of seats, enabling the Liberal Party under Justin Trudeau to form another minority government.
As a result, party members were undecided on whether he should continue as leader.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-54)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-55) On October 5, the Conservative caucus voted to adopt the provisions of the _Reform Act_, giving caucus the power to trigger a leadership review. O'Toole denied that it represented a threat to his leadership, insisting that the caucus was united as a team and that, as a supporter of the Act, he had encouraged his caucus to adopt all of its provisions.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-56)
texts.19:
### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Erin O'Toole (2020–2022)
On January 31, 2022, Conservative Calgary Heritage MP Bob Benzen submitted a letter with signatures from 35 Conservative MPs calling for a leadership review on O'Toole's leadership to the Conservative caucus chair, Scott Reid. In the letter, Benzen criticized O'Toole's reversal on repealing the Liberal government's carbon tax and assault weapons ban.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-57) On February 2, 2022, O'Toole was removed as leader by a margin of 73 to 45 votes.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-58)

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Second interim leadership (2022)
Then-deputy leader of the Conservative Party Candice Bergen was elected interim leader the same day O'Toole was ousted,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-59) and a leadership election was subsequently scheduled for September 10, 2022. Conservative MP and former cabinet minister Pierre Poilievre,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-runforpm-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-pierre-61) Conservative MP and former leadership candidate Leslyn Lewis,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-62) Independent (formerly Progressive Conservative) Member of Ontario Provincial Parliament Roman Baber,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-63) former leader of the now-defunct Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and former Premier of QuebecJean Charest,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-64) former MP, former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario, and Mayor of BramptonPatrick Brown,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-65) former Conservative MP Leona Alleslev,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-66) former BC MLA and Conservative MP Marc Dalton, and former Huntsville mayor and Conservative MP Scott Aitchison announced their candidacies for the leadership.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-67) On May 2, 2022, the Party announced that the six verified candidates for the leadership would be Aitchison, Baber, Brown, Charest, Lewis, Poilievre.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-68)

texts.23:
### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
[edit]
On September 10, 2022, Pierre Poilievre won the leadership on the first ballot in a landslide, winning over 68% of the points.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-:7-71) On September 12, Poilievre gave his first speech to his caucus as leader.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-72) On April 28, 2025, the party would lose the 2025 Canadian federal election, despite making parliamentary gains through victories in places such as Ontario, such as the province's 905 area and southwestern region, and receiving over 40% of the popular vote for the first time in party history.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-73)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-74) The Conservatives also formed the largest Official Opposition in Canadian history.
texts.24:
### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
Poilievre however lost his own seat of Carleton to Liberal candidate Bruce Fanjoy, one of the few times a major party leader in Canada has been defeated in his own riding.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-loss-2025-76) There were also calls for Poilievre to resign as Conservative leader grew following the election result.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-78) Despite this, there was reportedly limited interest from the party's caucus in replacing him immediately after the election given their party's increase in the share of the vote, expansion of its political base in the Greater Toronto Area, and his own popularity with such across the country.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-79) Prominent Conservative Party MPs including Andrew Scheer, Shannon Stubbs, and former cabinet ministers Jason Kenney and James Moore also publicly supported his continued leadership after the election.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-80) Despite this, he was criticized by veteran and senior party members for his demeanour and campaign management that they cited as a reason for the party's loss of the election.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-81) Poilievre returned to Parliament in August 2025, following his victory in the Battle River—Crowfoot by-election.

### In opposition (2015–present)
#### Pierre Poilievre (2022–present)
On November 5, 2025, MP [Chris d'Entremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_d'Entremont "Chris d'Entremont") left the Conservative Party to join the Liberal Party of Canada, citing issues with Pierre Poilievre's leadership style and 'negative' approach to politics; this was followed by MP Michael Ma in December 2025, MP Matt Jeneroux in February 2026, and MP Marilyn Gladu in April 2026.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-82) At the party's convention in Calgary in January 2026, Poilievre received 87.4% support in a leadership review vote, vowing to remain as party leader.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-83)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-84)
texts.26:
## Principles and policies
[edit]
As a relatively young party with a mixed political heritage and history, the federal Conservatives are often described as a "big tent" party[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-CartyTent-85) in a similar manner to the federal Canadian Liberals by encompassing members and voters who hold a variety of philosophies, ideas and stances, albeit sitting within the centre-right to the right-wing of the political spectrum.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-House2015-86)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BlaisLaslier2016-87)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BittnerKoop2013b-88)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Canadian_Encyclopedia-4) Broadly, the party is defined as practicing the Canadian model of conservatism and fiscal conservatism. Some political observers have noted the two most dominant wings of the party traditionally represented Red Tory and Blue Tory ideologies,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-89) whereas others have argued that the party has become less internally defined by these labels and that the terms tend to be used by outsiders.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-90) Other smaller but visible factional beliefs espoused by individuals within the party have been described by media commentators as liberal conservative, social conservative, right-wing populist and libertarian conservative.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-91)
texts.27:
## Principles and policies
In an effort to create a cohesive platform following its creation, the Conservative Party declared its founding core philosophies and principles to be fiscal accountability, upholding individual rights and freedom, belief in constitutional monarchy, the institutions of Parliament and Canada's democratic process, support for strong national defence, law and order, and Canada's history and traditions, and equal treatment for all Canadians.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-ReferenceA-92)

## Regional conservative parties
After the 2007 budget was announced, the Progressive Conservative governments in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador accused the federal Conservatives of breaching the terms of the Atlantic Accord.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-129)
As a result, relations worsened between the federal government and the two provincial governments, leading Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Danny Williams to denounce the federal Conservatives, which gave rise to his ABC (Anything But Conservative) campaign in the 2008 election.
The National Council of the CPC is its "highest governing body".[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-hilltimes_Rana_20210321-130)Christina Mitas, a former Ontario Progressive ConservativeMPP, has served as President of the National Council since February 2026, when she was elected unanimously following the party's convention in Calgary.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-cpc_national_council-131)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-mitas_instagram_20260201-132) She succeeded Stephen Barber, who had held the position since 2023[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-133) and who in turn had succeeded Robert Batherson, president from 2021 to 2023.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-hilltimes_Rana_20210321-130)
The National Council has 21 seats, including four from Ontario, three from Quebec, two from British Columbia, two from Alberta, two from Saskatchewan, two from Manitoba, four from Atlantic Canada, and one from each of the three territories.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-hilltimes_Rana_20210321-130)
texts.42:
## Regional conservative parties
The Conservative Party has historically been strongest in the inland West as well as rural Ontario.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-The_Canadian_Encyclopedia_2021_u150-134)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-The_Canadian_Encyclopedia_2011_a407-135) The party is strongest particularly in the provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, where it holds 30 out of 34 and all 14 federal seats respectively.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-House_of_Commons_of_Canada_y518-136) It tends to be weaker in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, particularly Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-137)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-138)
There is no official youth wing of the Conservative Party of Canada. There have been several attempts to create one, but all have failed. Despite this the party sets its minimum membership and voting age at 14. The party does however have several affiliated campus clubs at various universities.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-139)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-140)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-141)

The **Conservative Party of Canada** (**CPC**; French: _Parti conservateur du Canada_; **_PCC_**), sometimes referred to as the **Tories**, is a federal political party in Canada. The party sits at the centre-right to right of the Canadian political spectrum, with their federal rival, the centre to centre-leftLiberal Party of Canada, positioned to their left.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Canadian_Encyclopedia-4) The Conservatives are defined as a "big tent" party, practicing "brokerage politics"[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-politics-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Brooks2004-8)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Johnson2016c-9)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Smith2014-10) and welcoming a broad variety of members, including "Red Tories" and "Blue Tories".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Wolak2014-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-BellKulchyski2013-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-GagnonTanguay2017-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-LewisEveritt2017-14)

The CPC was formed by the merger of the two main right-leaning parties, the Progressive Conservative Party (PC Party) and the Canadian Alliance. The PC Party's roots go back to the original Conservative Party of Canada, which had formed numerous governments dating back to Canadian Confederation in 1867. In the 1993 federal election, the PC Party's Western Canadian support transferred to the Reform Party, which later became the Canadian Alliance. When it became clear that neither the PC Party nor the Canadian Alliance could beat the incumbent Liberals that had governed since the 1993 election, an effort to unite the right-of-centre parties emerged. In 2003, the Canadian Alliance and the PCs merged, forming the Conservative Party of Canada.
During the Conservative Party's governance of Canada from 2006 to 2015, its economic policies included reducing sales tax, reducing income taxes, reducing business taxes, balancing the national budget, permitting the construction of several pipelines, and creating the tax-free savings account (TFSA) and the Universal Child Care Benefit. In social policy, the government eliminated the long-gun registry, introduced mandatory minimum sentences for violent crimes, and raised the age of consent to 16 years of age. Internationally it supported the State of Israel, withdrew Canada from the Kyoto Protocol, and negotiated the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-18)

Under its first leader, Stephen Harper, the party governed with two minority governments after the federal elections of 2006 and 2008. It then won a majority government in the 2011 federal election before being defeated in the 2015 federal election by a majority Liberal government led by Justin Trudeau. Despite winning a plurality of the vote in each election, the party remained as Official Opposition after losing the 2019 and 2021 elections under its second and third leaders, Andrew Scheer and [Erin O'Toole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_O'Toole "Erin O'Toole") respectively. Pierre Poilievre was elected leader in the 2022 leadership election, leading the party through the 2025 election, which it again lost to the Liberals, while retaining opposition status.
John A. Macdonald, Prime Minister (1867–1873, 1878–1891), Canada's first Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal-Conservative Party, one of the party's predecessors
The Conservative Party is political heir to a series of right-of-centre parties that have existed in Canada, beginning with the Upper Canada Tories of the nineteenth century. John A. Macdonald and George-Étienne Cartier later founded the Liberal-Conservative Party. The party became known simply as the Conservative Party after 1873, and the Progressive Conservative Party after 1942. Like its historical predecessors and conservative parties in some other Commonwealth nations (such as the Conservative Party of the United Kingdom), members of the present-day Conservative Party of Canada are sometimes referred to as "Tories".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada#cite_note-Tories-roots-19) The modern Conservative Party of Canada is also legal heir to the heritage of the historical conservative parties by virtue of assuming the assets and liabilities of the former Progressive Conservative Party upon the merger of 2003.
